data/images/Adrenal_Gland_Pathology_Segm: The slide shows a purple-pink microscopic tissue image behind the title “Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 Overview.” It lists “DAVID M. PINSON, DVM, PHD” and “PROFESSOR OF CLINICAL PATHOLOGY, PEORIA,” with “THE UNIVERSITY OF ILLINOIS COLLEGE OF MEDICINE” at the bottom. The nearby text describes this as an introductory overview providing a limited physiologic and pathologic framework for understanding adrenal disease.

The slide is titled “Learning Objectives” and lists two goals: identify regulation and control mechanisms of adrenocortical function and approaches for pharmacological intervention; and specify the biochemistry, physiology, and pathology of catecholamines and stimuli that modulate adrenomedullary function. LO1–LO5 cover hypercortisolism, Cushing’s disease, adrenal androgen oversecretion and virilizing disorders, hypocortisolism, and Addison’s disease and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. LO6 addresses adrenal medulla neoplasms (pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma) and paragangliomas; LO7 addresses multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome, including clinical, laboratory, and morphologic features and prognosis. The nearby text frames the session around adrenal gland hyperfunction or hypofunction, enzyme abnormalities, and functional or nonfunctional adrenal tumors.

The slide titled “Microlecture Series” contains a table with columns “Segment,” “Title,” and “Duration”: Segment 1 — Overview — 4 min 46 sec; Segment 2 — Adrenal Hyperfunction — 17 min 13 sec; Segment 3 — Adrenal Hypofunction — 14 min 35 sec; Segment 4 — Adrenal Neoplasia — 10 min 01 sec. It outlines a four-part series on adrenal topics, with the overview as the first segment.

The slide titled “Adrenal Gland Histology” shows adrenal tissue labeled capsule, glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis, Cortex, and Medulla, with the mnemonic labels “Salt,” “Sugar,” and “Sex” above the cortical layers. A table pairs zona glomerulosa with “mineralocorticoids (aldosterone),” zona fasciculata with “glucocorticoids (cortisol),” zona reticularis with “sex steroids (androgens),” and Medulla with “catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine).” The “Mnemonic Hint” reads “GFR = glomerular filtration rate = glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis = salt, sugar, sex,” linking adrenal layers to their hormones and functions.

The slide, “Adrenal Cortical Hormones,” maps synthetic pathways under “Zona Glomerulosa,” “Zona Fasciculata,” and “Zona Reticularis,” from cholesterol through labeled intermediates to aldosterone, cortisol, androgens, and estrogens. The enzyme key reads “3β = 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase,” “11β(B1) = 11β hydroxylase,” “17α = 17α hydroxylase,” “18 = hydroxyl → aldehyde at position 18,” and “21 = 21 hydroxylase”; the nearby text highlights 21-hydroxylase and states that its deficiency is an important cause of adrenal hyperplasia and a virulizing syndrome.

The slide titled “Adrenal Medulla Catecholamines” shows a biochemical pathway from tyrosine through Dopa, dopamine, and norepinephrine to epinephrine, with enzyme labels “Tyrosine hydroxylase,” “Dopa decarboxylase,” “Dopamine β-hydroxylase,” and “Phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase.” A side pathway shows tyramine and octopamine, with labels “L-Amino acid decarboxylase” and “Hepatic hydroxylase”; the nearby text says the adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine and that intermediates are also important neurotransmitters.

The slide, titled “Cortisol Concentrations are Diurnal,” shows a line graph with “Cortisol, ng/ml” on the y-axis and “Time of Day” on the x-axis, marked Midnight, 3 AM, 6 AM, 9 AM, 12 Noon, 3 PM, 6 PM, 9 PM, and Midnight. The curve rises to a morning peak and then declines through the day; the bullets read: “Cortisol values vary with time of day,” “Reference ranges vary with time of day,” and “Loss of diurnal variation is clinically significant.” The concept is that cortisol secretion varies over the day, and loss of this cycling can be significant even when laboratory values are within the reference range.

The slide, titled “Laboratory Testing Framed in Physiology,” lists serum cortisol, salivary cortisol, urine cortisol, urine metabolites, serum ACTH, ACTH stimulation test, low dose Dex* suppression, high dose Dex* suppression, serum aldosterone, serum renin, serum osmolality, serum electrolytes, urinary electrolytes, urine Metanephrines, and urine vanillylmandelic acid; “*Dexamethasone” is printed below. A diagram shows “Corticotropin Releasing Hormone (CRH)” acting on the “Pituitary,” which releases “Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH)” toward the adrenal gland, with “Inhibition” also labeled; the adrenal tissue illustration is labeled “Aldosterone,” “Glucocorticoids,” “Androgens,” “Salt,” “Sugar,” and “Sex,” and a separate box shows “Renin (kidney)” → “Angiotensin I” → “Angiotensin II.” The slide illustrates that adrenal testing is framed by physiologic regulation and includes tests of adrenal hormones and related analytes.

The slide “Summary of Adrenal Pathology” organizes adrenal gland cortex–medulla disease into three categories: “Hyperfunction,” “Hypofunction,” and “Tumors/Proliferative Lesions,” with each category further identified as primary versus secondary or functional versus nonfunctional. The listed diseases include Cushing syndrome, Cushing disease, Aldosteronism, “Virulizing syndromes”; acute and chronic adrenal insufficiency, “Waterhouse - Fredichsen,” and abrupt cessation of steroid Rx; and pituitary microadenomas → adrenal hyperplasia, cortical hyperplasia, cortical adenoma/carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, MEN syndromes, and metastatic neoplasia. The concept is that adrenal pathology is grouped by excess function, deficient function, or proliferative lesions; the nearby text says clinical presentation depends on which hormones are in excess or deficient and on co-morbidities.
data/images/B7W1_Growth_Hormone_Physiolo: The diagram shows the “hypothalamic-pituitaryliver axis”: the hypothalamus sends “Growth hormone-releasing hormone” (under “Releasing Hormone”) and “Somatostatin” (under “Release-inhibiting Hormone”) to the pituitary “Somatotrope (cell type),” which releases “Growth Hormone” toward the liver, leading to “IGF-1.” Green plus and red minus signs mark stimulatory and inhibitory effects; dashed feedback paths with minus signs indicate inhibition by IGF-1, and glucose is not shown.

The diagram, titled “Summary of factors that regulate GH secretion,” places “GH secretion” at the center and shows factors connected by arrows. Green plus signs indicate stimulation by “Hormonal” factors—“Estrogen,” “Thyroid hormone,” and “Ghrelin”—“Amino acids (arginine),” “Stress” (“Neurogenic,” “Physical”), “Exercise,” and “Hypoglycemia”; red minus signs indicate inhibition by “Aging” and “Hyperglycemia.” It summarizes factors that increase or decrease growth hormone secretion.

The graph plots “Growth hormone (µg/liter)” over time, with labels “8am,” “8pm,” “Midnight,” and “4am,” and a bracket labeled “Sleep.” Levels show intermittent peaks, including prominent peaks during sleep; nearby text states “Limited clinical utility of measuring serum GH levels” because of “Pulsatile secretion,” “Short half life,” and “Diurnal rhythm of secretion,” with “Peak secretion in early morning before awakening” and “Lowest secretion during the day.”

The diagram shows GH signaling from the hypothalamus/anterior pituitary to the liver and bone; the liver is labeled “IGF-1,” “IGF-BP3,” and “ALS,” and an “IGF-1” arrow points to bone with the label “Endocrine.” The bone is also labeled “Paracrine,” with “PTH” and “Estradiol” shown beside it, and the outcome is “Increased linear growth”; the slide states, “Most of the effects of GH on bone are mediated through IGF-1 (endocrine action).” Nearby text notes that GH also has some direct effects on bone and that local IGF-1 can be produced without GH through paracrine actions or other hormones such as PTH or estradiol.
data/images/Drugs_for_Diabetes-2025-STUD: The graph shows plasma insulin concentration during an infusion of glucose, comparing “Normal subjects,” “Type 2 diabetics,” and “Type 1 diabetics.” The y-axis is “Plasma concentration of insulin (μU/mL)” (0, 40, and 80), and the x-axis is “Minutes” (0, 5, and 10); the normal-subject curve rises sharply, the Type 2 curve rises more gradually, and the Type 1 curve stays low. It illustrates differences in insulin response during glucose infusion, alongside the page text describing Type 1 as little to no insulin secretion and Type 2 as insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency.

The diagram, titled “Target Sites of Anti-Diabetic Agents,” shows the kidney, pancreas, brain/CNS, liver, muscle and fat, and gut, with arrows converging on “↓ Glucose level”; there are no axes. The site labels are “Renal Glucose Retention,” “β-Cell & α-Cell Dysfunction,” “CNS (Dys)Regulation,” “Hepatic Glucose overproduction,” “Insulin Resistance,” and “Glucose Absorption & Loss of Incretin Effect.” Drug classes listed include SGLT2 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, meglitinides, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1R & GLP-1R/GIPR agonists, bromocriptine, biguanides, TZDs, and α-glucosidase inhibitors; the diagram teaches which sites and processes these agents target to lower glucose level.

A patient-centered T2DM care wheel surrounds a patient icon and lists: “Refer for DSMES, MNT, lifestyle changes,” “Identify and manage T2DM complications and comorbidities,” “Manage T2DM pharmacotherapy,” “Set SMART goals with patient,” “Monitor: glycemic status, weight, blood pressure, lipids, renal function,” and “Identify social determinants and barriers.” The adjacent text says, “Pharmacotherapy for T2DM is guided by patient-centered treatment factors and comorbidities, including:” risk or presence of ASCVD, presence of CKD, and presence of HF. Nearby text also asks, “Which agent to start --- think about the patient's co-morbidities”.

A black-and-white portrait shows a young child wrapped in a blanket, facing the camera. The nearby text reads “The Miracle of Insulin”; the image has no visible labels or axes.

The graph, titled “Normal Insulin Secretion,” plots “Serum Insulin” against “Time (Hours)” from 0 to 24; the y-axis is marked 0 to 50. A yellow curve rises after the three arrows labeled “Meal,” showing meal-related peaks over a dark blue band labeled “Basal (background) Insulin” and triangular peaks labeled “Bolus (meal) Insulin,” illustrating basal insulin secretion plus meal-associated boluses.

The diagram shows human proinsulin as a green “C-peptide” connecting the orange “A chain” and “B chain”; the orange chains are identified in the nearby text as insulin. Amino-acid abbreviations and residue numbers are shown, along with S–S links between the chains; the nearby text identifies the concept as the structure of proinsulin and insulin and mentions “Differences in the A and B chains.”

“Pharmacokinetic Profiles of Insulins” is a graph of glucose infusion rate (mg/kg/min) versus Time (h), with curves labeled “Insulin lispro, aspart, glulisine,” “Regular,” “NPH,” “Insulin detemir,” “Insulin degludec,” and “Insulin glargine.” It compares the extent and duration of insulin action; the accompanying text says durations shown are typical of an average dose of 0.2-0.3 U/kg and that the durations of regular and NPH insulin increase considerably when dosage is increased.

The “Basal/Bolus Treatment” diagram shows three green peaks labeled “Rapid (lispro, aspart, glulisine, inhaled)” above Breakfast, Lunch, and Dinner, and a turquoise line labeled “Degludec, detemir, or glargine” extending across the timeline toward Bed. The horizontal time labels include 8:00, 12:00, 16:00, 20:00, 24:00, 4:00, and 8:00; no axis title or units are shown. It illustrates rapid-acting insulin doses around meals alongside a long-acting insulin treatment across the day and night.

The image shows a wearable insulin pump clipped to jeans and connected by tubing to a circular device on the abdomen. Nearby text reads “Insulin Delivery Systems,” “Injectors,” “Injection Aids,” “Pen delivery,” and “Insulin Pump”; there are no axes. It illustrates an insulin pump delivery system.

Two side-by-side portraits show a woman with a fuller-looking face on the left and a thinner-looking face on the right. The diagram is labeled “LOW BLOOD GLUCOSE (Blood glucose less than 40 mg/dl)” and shows the hypothalamic regulatory center signaling through the pituitary, adrenal gland, autonomic nervous system, and pancreas; insulin is crossed out, and the hormone labels include ACTH, cortisol, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and glucagon. The table lists “Glyco-genolysis” as 0 for cortisol, +++ for the epinephrine/norepinephrine column, and ++ for glucagon; “Gluconeo-genesis” is ++, 0, and ++, respectively. It illustrates hormonal responses to low blood glucose; the nearby text asks, “Symptoms of moderate to severe hypoglycemia?”

The chart shows blood glucose on a vertical axis labeled “[Blood glucose], mg/dl,” scaled from 0 to 100. As glucose falls, “Insulin production decreases,” “Epinephrine and glucagon production increases,” “Growth hormone production increases,” and “Cortisol production increases”; the arrows mark these changes along the scale. It also shows “Adrenergic symptoms begin:” anxiety, palpitation, tremor, and sweating, and “Neuroglycopenia symptoms begin:” headache, confusion, slurred speech, seizures, coma, and death.

A vertical scale labeled “Blood glucose (mg/100 mL)” runs from 0 to 100, with a bracket marking the “Normal range” at about 60–90. The chart lists “Subtle neurological signs; hunger,” “Release of glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol,” “Sweating, trembling,” “Lethargy,” “Convulsions, coma,” “Permanent brain damage (if prolonged),” and “Death” at progressively lower glucose levels; nearby text says the main blood-glucose regulators are insulin, glucagon, and epinephrine, in the context of symptoms of moderate to severe hypoglycemia.

The image shows three glucagon products: a device labeled “Gvoke HypoPen (glucagon injection),” a nasal product labeled “Baqsimi” and “3 mg / device,” and a third injection device with partly unclear labeling. The nearby text states: “Indicated as a treatment for severe hypoglycemia, which may occur in patients with diabetes mellitus. Anatomy of the pituitary gland.” and it teaches the gland’s anatomy and its spatial relationships to surrounding structures.

An axial computed tomography image of the head shows a white arrow pointing to a small bright area near the center of the brain. The caption reads, “Figure 2. Macroadenoma (arrow) on computed tomography.”

A sagittal MRI shows the pituitary region with a vertical measurement marker labeled “18.74mm”; no axes are shown. The nearby text states that prolactin “250 mcg per L [10,870 pmol per L] or more” suggests prolactinoma, while “greater than 500 mcg per L (21,739 pmol per L)” is diagnostic for macroprolactinoma (98% specificity, 35% sensitivity).

The flowchart, titled “Approach to the Evaluation and Management of a Pituitary Incidentaloma,” begins with “Discovery of incidental pituitary adenoma”; if the mass is found on CT, it says “perform MRI,” and it directs physical examination and laboratory tests to determine pituitary hormonal status. The tests listed are “prolactin, IGF-1, LH/FSH, TSH/free T₄, 24-hour urine free cortisol, testosterone [men], estradiol [women].” Nonfunctioning tumors branch into “Macroadenoma (≥ 1 cm)” and “Microadenoma (< 1 cm),” with visual-field testing, neurosurgery referral when indicated, and follow-up MRI and laboratory testing; follow-up branches address “No changes,” “Increase in size,” and “Changes in laboratory test results.” Functioning tumors branch into “GH- or ACTH-secreting tumor” (refer to neurosurgery and endocrinology) or “Prolactinoma” (treat with dopamine agonists if indicated; refer to endocrinology); the diagram also asks “Abutting optic chiasm or ≥ 1 cm in size?” and defines abbreviations in a footnote.
